english: to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves)
usage: The subject is almost always 가슴(이) or 심장(이) — the heart, not the person. Say 가슴이 두근거려요, not 저는 두근거려요.
I'm so worked up because of the interview
Works for both happy excitement (a date, a concert) and anxious nerves (an interview, exam results) — context decides which.
examples: 발표 직전이라 심장이 두근거려요.
It's right before my presentation, so my heart is racing.
심장이 두근거리다 and 가슴이 두근거리다 are interchangeable; 가슴 sounds slightly softer.
내일 그 사람 만난다고 생각하니까 벌써 두근거려.
Just thinking about meeting them tomorrow, my heart's already fluttering.
Casual 두근거려 to a close friend. 두근두근 is the matching mimetic word you'll see in texts.
커피를 너무 많이 마셔서 가슴이 두근거렸어요.
I drank too much coffee, so my heart was pounding.
Also used literally for a physical racing heart from caffeine or running, not just emotion.
nuance: 두근거리다 describes the physical sensation of a pounding or fluttering heart, so the grammatical subject is 가슴/심장, while the person is marked with -은/는 or a cause phrase. It covers the full range from giddy anticipation to nervous dread, which is why Koreans pair it with 설레다 for good nerves or 긴장되다 for bad ones to disambiguate. The mimetic 두근두근 shows up constantly in casual writing and captions.
mistakes: Saying 저는 두근거려요 to mean 'I'm excited' — the heart is the subject, so use 가슴이 두근거려요 (or 저는 설레요 if you mean the feeling).
Imperative/propositive forms like 두근거리세요 are grammatically possible but sound odd in real life, since you can't really order someone's heart to pound.

english: to miss / to long for (someone or something absent)
usage: 그립다 is an adjective, so the thing you miss takes -이/가, not -을/를: 고향이 그리워요, not 고향을 그리워요.
There are many times I miss my family
Living abroad, this is the natural way to talk about homesickness for people, places, food, or a past time.
examples: 한국에 산 지 일 년 됐는데 가끔 엄마 음식이 그리워요.
It's been a year living in Korea, and sometimes I miss my mom's cooking.
ㅂ-irregular: 그립- + -어요 → 그리워요. Very common for expats describing home food.
그 시절이 정말 그리웠어요.
I really missed those days.
Past tense 그리웠어요 for looking back nostalgically on a period of life.
친구가 너무 그리워서 영상통화를 했어.
I missed my friend so much that I made a video call.
그리워서 (because I missed) drives an action. To say someone actively misses, switch to the verb 그리워하다.
nuance: 그립다 is an adjective expressing your own felt longing, so what you miss is the subject (-이/가) and you cannot attach a direct object. To describe a third person missing something ('he misses home'), Korean shifts to the verb 그리워하다, since adjectives can't report others' inner feelings directly. Compare it with 보고 싶다, which is the everyday, conversational way to say you miss seeing a person; 그립다 sounds more wistful and literary.
mistakes: Marking the object with -을/를 (고향을 그리워요) — as an adjective it needs -이/가: 고향이 그리워요.
Using 그립다 to say someone else misses something; switch to 그리워하다 (동생이 고향을 그리워해요).

english: to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed
usage: Covers two senses: bashful shyness (meeting new people) and embarrassment over a mistake. Tone and context separate them.
The verb form 부끄러워하다 is used to tell someone else not to be shy or to describe a shy person.
examples: 사람들 앞에서 한국어로 말하는 게 아직 부끄러워요.
I'm still shy about speaking Korean in front of people.
ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽- + -어요 → 부끄러워요. A very relatable expat sentence.
실수해서 너무 부끄러웠어요.
I made a mistake and was so embarrassed.
Past 부끄러웠어요 for embarrassment over something you did.
동생이 낯선 사람을 부끄러워해요.
My younger sibling is shy around strangers.
For describing someone else's shyness, use the verb 부끄러워하다 + object.
nuance: 부끄럽다 spans shy bashfulness and self-conscious embarrassment, but it leans gentler and more inward than 창피하다, which is sharper public mortification. Because it's an adjective, your own feeling takes -이/가 on the cause, and describing another person's shyness requires the verb 부끄러워하다. The noun 부끄러움 means 'shyness' or 'shame' and shows up in more formal or written contexts.
mistakes: Using 부끄럽다 for strong public humiliation; 창피하다 hits harder for 'mortified'.
Trying to say 'he is shy' with the plain adjective — use 부끄러워하다 for third-person feelings.

english: to be embarrassing / to feel mortified
usage: The go-to word when you've made a fool of yourself in public — louder and more intense than 부끄럽다.
-아/어 죽겠어요 ('dying of ~') is an extremely common intensifier with feeling words.
examples: 넘어진 게 너무 창피해서 빨리 일어났어요.
I was so mortified about falling that I got up fast.
하다-verb: 창피하- + -아요 → 창피해요. Classic public-embarrassment scenario.
사람들이 다 쳐다봐서 창피했어요.
Everyone was staring, so I was embarrassed.
Past 창피했어요. Note the cause is usually a public situation.
그렇게 큰 소리로 말하면 내가 창피하잖아.
If you talk that loudly, you embarrass me.
Used to tell someone they're embarrassing you; 창피하잖아 adds a mild complaining tone.
nuance: 창피하다 is the stronger, more public sibling of 부끄럽다 — it's the 'I want the floor to swallow me' feeling after you trip in front of a crowd or get scolded openly. It describes either your own mortification (저 창피해요) or a situation that causes it (창피한 상황). 쪽팔리다 is the very casual, slangy equivalent friends use among themselves, but it's too rough for polite settings.
mistakes: Swapping in the slang 쪽팔리다 in formal or work situations — keep 창피하다 there.
Forgetting the contraction: 창피하- + -아요 becomes 창피해요, not 창피하아요.

english: to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous
usage: Use it when something is so unexpected or nonsensical that you're left speechless — both the event and your reaction.
황당한 + noun describes a ridiculous situation, story, or excuse.
examples: 갑자기 예약이 취소됐다고 해서 너무 황당했어요.
They suddenly said my reservation was canceled, so I was dumbfounded.
하다-verb: 황당하- + -았어요 → 황당했어요. Common in customer-service mishaps.
그 사람 변명이 너무 황당해서 웃음이 나왔어.
His excuse was so absurd that I burst out laughing.
황당해서 (because it was absurd) leading to a reaction. Casual with a friend.
황당한 표정으로 나를 쳐다봤어요.
They looked at me with a dumbfounded expression.
황당한 표정 ('a stunned/what-the-heck face') is a set phrase you'll hear a lot.
nuance: 황당하다 captures the 'wait, what?' feeling when something is so unexpected or illogical it leaves you stunned — a baffling excuse, an out-of-nowhere cancellation, an absurd demand. It describes both the ridiculous thing itself and your reaction to it. It overlaps heavily with 어이없다, but 황당하다 leans toward 'bizarre/unbelievable,' while 어이없다 leans toward 'so dumb it's offensive.'
mistakes: Translating it as plain 'surprised' (놀라다) — 황당하다 specifically implies the thing was absurd or nonsensical, not just unexpected.
Overusing it for mild surprises; save it for genuinely ridiculous situations.

english: to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless
usage: This is unbelievable / I can't even
The everyday reaction when something is so dumb or unfair it leaves you speechless. Extremely common in casual speech.
I'm so dumbfounded I can't speak
The full form 어이가 없다 is often used; the 가 can drop in fast speech.
examples: 새치기를 하길래 진짜 어이없었어요.
Someone cut in line, so I was totally flabbergasted.
없다-type adjective: 어이없- + -었어요 → 어이없었어요. Note 길래 = 'because (I saw/noticed).'
그 말 듣고 너무 어이없어서 헛웃음이 나왔어.
After hearing that, I was so dumbfounded I let out a dry laugh.
Pairs naturally with 헛웃음 (a hollow/dry laugh). Casual register.
어이없는 변명 좀 그만해.
Stop with the ridiculous excuses.
어이없는 + noun ('a ludicrous ~'). 어이없는 변명/상황 are common collocations.
nuance: 어이없다 (also said as 어이가 없다) is the punchy, everyday way Koreans react to something so absurd, unfair, or stupid that it stuns them into a speechless half-laugh. Compared with 황당하다, it carries a touch more exasperation or contempt — it's what you mutter when someone cuts in line or gives a nonsense excuse. Because 없다 behaves like an adjective, the third-person verb form is 어이없어하다.
mistakes: Spelling or hearing it as 어의없다 — the word is 어이 (no ㄴ/ㅢ); standard spelling is 어이없다.
Using it for pleasant surprise; 어이없다 is always negative — bafflement mixed with annoyance.

english: to be thrilling / to feel an electric, tingling rush
usage: For exhilarating moments — a roller coaster, a buzzer-beater, a sudden win. Has a sense of electric, tingling excitement.
짜릿한 + noun: 짜릿한 순간 (a thrilling moment), 짜릿한 경기 (a nail-biter of a game).
examples: 역전골이 터지는 순간 진짜 짜릿했어요.
The moment the comeback goal went in, it was such a rush.
하다-verb: 짜릿하- + -았어요 → 짜릿했어요. Sports are the classic context.
롤러코스터 탈 때 그 짜릿한 느낌이 좋아.
I love that electric thrill when riding a roller coaster.
짜릿한 느낌/스릴 are natural collocations. Casual with a friend.
찬물로 샤워하니까 짜릿했어요.
Taking a cold shower felt tingly and invigorating.
Also used for the literal tingling jolt of cold or a mild electric sensation, not only emotional thrills.
nuance: 짜릿하다 originally describes a literal tingling, electric sensation (a mild shock, a cold splash) and extends to the metaphorical thrill of exhilarating moments — a comeback win, a thrill ride, a daring success. It's overwhelmingly positive and intense, the high-adrenaline cousin of 신나다 (fun/upbeat). You'll see it paired with 스릴 (thrill) and in ad copy promising an exciting experience.
mistakes: Using it for ordinary mild fun; 짜릿하다 implies a sharp, intense rush, so 재미있다/신나다 fit calmer enjoyment.
Forgetting the double ㅉ and tense ㅌ in spelling: 짜릿하다, not 자릿하다.

english: to feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close
usage: I'm a little hurt / let down
A soft, relationship-based hurt when someone you care about falls short of your expectations — not anger, more disappointment.
Please don't take it the wrong way / don't feel hurt
A set phrase to reassure someone you didn't mean to slight them.
examples: 생일인데 연락도 안 해서 좀 섭섭했어요.
It was my birthday and you didn't even text, so I felt a bit hurt.
하다-verb: 섭섭하- + -았어요 → 섭섭했어요. Classic mild-grievance use.
벌써 간다니까 섭섭하네요.
Hearing you're already leaving makes me feel sad to see you go.
Also expresses the bittersweet sadness of a goodbye, not just grievance. -네요 adds soft emotion.
네가 그렇게 말하니까 진짜 섭섭하다.
When you talk like that, it really hurts my feelings.
Plain 섭섭하다 ending to a close friend, voicing gentle hurt.
nuance: 섭섭하다 is a uniquely Korean shade of feeling: a gentle, wistful hurt or letdown when someone close to you doesn't meet your emotional expectations, or the bittersweet pang of parting. It's softer than 서운하다 (its near-synonym) only by nuance — many use them interchangeably — and much milder than anger or 화나다. Telling someone 섭섭해 signals 'you let me down a little,' inviting reassurance rather than confrontation.
mistakes: Treating it as anger; 섭섭하다 is tender disappointment, so 화나다/짜증나다 are wrong for this feeling.
Using it about strangers — it implies a relationship close enough to have expectations.

english: to be sick of / to get fed up with something
usage: The thing you're fed up with takes -에 or -이/가: 라면에 질렸어요 or 라면이 질렸어요 (both heard).
I ate it until I got sick of it
질릴 만큼 ('to the point of getting tired of it') is a common way to say 'way too much.'
examples: 매일 라면만 먹으니까 이제 진짜 질렸어요.
Eating only ramen every day, I'm really sick of it now.
이-stem verb: 질리- + -었어요 → 질렸어요. Marker -에 (라면에) is the textbook choice.
똑같은 일상에 질려서 여행을 떠났어.
I got fed up with the same routine, so I took off on a trip.
질려서 (fed up, so) → action. -에 marks the thing you tired of.
그 노래 너무 많이 들어서 질릴 정도예요.
I've heard that song so much it's at the point of being sick of it.
질릴 정도 ('to the point of being fed up') is a useful set phrase.
nuance: 질리다 is the everyday verb for being so over-saturated with something — a food, a routine, a song — that you can't stand any more of it. It also has a second, scarier sense: 질리다 can mean to turn pale or be paralyzed with fear (겁에 질리다, 새파랗게 질리다), so context matters. For the 'fed up' meaning, mark the source with -에 (most standard) or -이/가; English-speakers often wrongly add -을/를.
mistakes: Marking the source with -을/를; use -에 (라면에 질렸어요) or -이/가.
Forgetting the second meaning — 겁에 질리다 / 얼굴이 질리다 means to go pale with fear, not 'be bored.'

english: to be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation
usage: I'm so excited / my heart is fluttering
Happy, fluttery anticipation — a trip, a date, a first day. The positive counterpart to nervous 긴장되다.
I waited with a fluttering, excited heart
설레는 + noun (마음, 기분) is a very common collocation for hopeful anticipation.
examples: 내일 여행 가는 생각에 벌써 설레요.
Just thinking about the trip tomorrow, I'm already giddy with excitement.
설레- + -어요 contracts to 설레요. Note: standard dictionary form is 설레다, not 설레이다.
첫 데이트라서 너무 설렜어요.
It was a first date, so my heart was really fluttering.
Past 설렜어요 (설레 + 었 → 설렜). One of the most-loved feeling words in K-dramas.
설레지 마, 그냥 친구로 만나는 거야.
Don't get your hopes fluttering, we're just meeting as friends.
Casual 설레지 마 teasing someone not to read too much into it.
nuance: 설레다 is the warm, fluttery thrill of looking forward to something good — the butterflies before a date, a trip, or a fresh start. The standard dictionary form is 설레다 (past 설렜어요); you'll hear and see 설레이다/설레인다 everywhere, but those are nonstandard, so write 설레요/설렜어요. The matching noun 설렘 ('the flutter of excitement') is hugely popular in captions and song lyrics.
mistakes: Writing 설레이다 / 설레여요 / 설레임 — these are nonstandard; the correct forms are 설레다 / 설레요 / 설렘.
Confusing the contraction: 설레 + 었어요 = 설렜어요, not 설레었어요 in natural speech.

english: to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement
usage: A buzzy, can't-sit-still excitement before something fun — a holiday, a concert, a trip. Often a bit giddier and more restless than 설레다.
들뜬 + noun: 들뜬 마음, 들뜬 분위기 — a giddy atmosphere, like a Friday night out.
examples: 휴가 앞두고 다들 들떠 있어요.
With the vacation coming up, everyone's all keyed up.
ㅡ-irregular: 들뜨- + -어요 → 들떠요. 들떠 있다 = 'be in a giddy state.'
연휴라서 그런지 마음이 들떴어요.
Maybe because it's a long weekend, I felt giddy and restless.
Past 들떴어요 (들뜨 + 었 → 들떴). The cause is often a holiday or event.
너무 들뜨지 말고 짐부터 챙기자.
Don't get too carried away — let's pack first.
들뜨지 말다 ('don't get over-excited'), often a gentle reminder to stay grounded.
nuance: 들뜨다 is the bubbly, restless excitement that lifts your mood before something fun, but it carries a faint undertone of being so giddy you're a little distracted or unsettled — which is why 너무 들뜨지 마 ('don't get carried away') is a common caution. Compared with 설레다 (sweet, heart-fluttering anticipation), 들뜨다 is more buzzy and outwardly hyped. It conjugates as a ㅡ-irregular: 들뜨- + -어 → 들떠.
mistakes: Botching the ㅡ-drop: 들뜨- + -어요 is 들떠요, not 들뜨어요.
Assuming it's purely positive — it can hint at being overexcited or not thinking clearly, hence the 'don't get carried away' nuance.

english: to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back
usage: Don't let it intimidate you / don't shrink back
Often used as encouragement. The phrase is built from 주눅(이) 들다, so you'll also see 주눅이 들다.
I got intimidated by the atmosphere
The cause takes -에: 분위기에, 사람들 앞에서 주눅들다 — to feel small in a tense or high-pressure setting.
examples: 한국어 실력이 부족해서 회의 때 자꾸 주눅들어요.
My Korean isn't good enough, so I keep getting cowed in meetings.
ㄹ-irregular: before -ㅂ니다 the ㄹ drops → 주눅듭니다. A very real expat workplace feeling.
면접관 앞에서 너무 주눅들었어요.
I felt completely intimidated in front of the interviewer.
Past 주눅들었어요. 주눅(이) 들다 literally means your spirit shrinks.
주눅들지 말고 당당하게 말해.
Don't shrink back — speak up confidently.
주눅들지 말다 paired with 당당하게 ('confidently'), the opposite attitude. Common pep-talk.
nuance: 주눅들다 (from 주눅(이) 들다) means to feel so intimidated or self-conscious that you shrink back, lose confidence, and can't assert yourself — a very useful word for the expat experience of freezing up in Korean meetings or formal settings. It's a ㄹ-irregular built on 들다, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ endings (주눅듭니다). The natural cure-words to pair it with are 당당하다 (be self-assured) and the encouragement 주눅들지 마.
mistakes: Keeping the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다 (saying 주눅들습니다) — the ㄹ drops: 주눅듭니다.
Marking the cause with -을/를; use -에 (분위기에 주눅들다).
